claim: Male C57BL/6N mice were obtained from the NIA Aging Mouse Colony (Charles River Laboratories, Kingston, NY).
source: Male C57BL/6N mice were obtained from the NIA Aging Mouse Colony (Charles River Laboratories, Kingston, NY).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the source and strain of mice used in the study.

claim: Under well-controlled environmental conditions, laboratory mice can live up to 4 years.
source: Under well-controlled environmental conditions, laboratory mice can live up to 4 years (Miller et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miller et al., 2002.

claim: The frailty index (FI) increased linearly as a function of age, with age accounting for 61.5% of FI variation.
source: The FI increased linearly as a function of age (Figure 1B, p=3.80e-16, r2 = 0.615), with age accounting for 61.5% of FI variation.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing correlation between FI and age with p-value and r-squared value.

claim: Gait speed exhibited the strongest relationship with FI, with FI explaining approximately 33% of the gait speed decrease.
source: Gait speed exhibited the strongest relationship with FI from that of age itself, since FI can explain ~33% of the gait speed decrease (Figure 1G)
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical analysis and refers to Figure 1G showing the relationship.

claim: After adjusting for age, frailty lost the association with gait speed.
source: After adjusting for age, frailty lost the association with gait speed (Figure 1G, p=0.477)
evidence: Statistical analysis showing loss of significance after age adjustment.

claim: Blood glucose, plasma insulin concentrations, and HOMA-IR index were largely similar from 6 to 16 months and were observed to be lower after 19 months of age.
source: Blood glucose, plasma insulin concentrations, and HOMA-IR index, a surrogate for estimating insulin resistance (Matthews et al., 1985), were largely similar from 6 to 16 months and were observed to be lower after 19 months of age (Figure 1K,L, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns in metabolic markers with reference to figures.

claim: Body weight and whole-body fat percentage showed a steady increase in values up to approximately 19 months and a decline thereafter.
source: Group differences in body weight and whole-body fat percentage were noted with a steady increase in values up to ~19 months and a decline thereafter (p=7.87e-07, r2 = 0.319 and p=2.71e–07, r2 = 0.340, respectively)
evidence: Statistical analysis of body composition changes with age.

claim: The subcutaneous/visceral fat ratio revealed a linear reduction in visceral adiposity as a function of age.
source: To determine body fat distribution, a 7T MRI body scanner was used to quantify the subcutaneous/visceral fat ratio, which revealed a linear reduction in visceral adiposity as a function of age (p=3.38e-05, r2 = 0.2996) (Figure 2B).
evidence: MRI-based measurement with statistical analysis.

claim: Old mice exhibited marked and significantly lower femoral cortical bone thickness and trabecular bone mineral density compared to the other two groups of mice.
source: Old mice exhibited marked and significantly lower femoral cortical bone thickness (p=7.20e-07, r2 = 0.458) and trabecular bone mineral density (BMD) (p=0.0184, r2 = 0.112) compared to the other two groups of mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Micro-CT measurements with statistical comparisons between age groups.

claim: The energetic cost of walking increased exponentially from approximately 20 months of age and was paralleled by a sustained decrease in work capacity.
source: Remarkably, the energetic cost of walking increased exponentially from ~20 months of age and was paralleled by a sustained decrease in work capacity (Figure 2D, 1st and 4th panels).
evidence: Metabolic treadmill data showing age-related changes in energetic parameters.

claim: RER and heat dissipation values decreased from approximately 0.85 to approximately 0.80, and from 5 to 3 kJ h−1, respectively, indicating higher utilization of lipid than glucose as an energy source.
source: Interestingly, RER and heat dissipation values, obtained during the treadmill monitoring, decreased from ~0.85 to ~0.80, and from 5 to 3 kJ h−1, respectively, indicating higher utilization of lipid than glucose as an energy source, and less heat dissipation in the older groups of animals (Figure 2D, 3rd and 2nd panels).
evidence: Metabolic measurements indicating substrate utilization patterns.

claim: Frailty status was more apparent with age as gait velocity increases.
source: Frailty status was more apparent with age as gait velocity increases: Specifically, at younger ages, the frailty index was inversely correlated with gait velocity while at older ages frailty status showed strong association with lower gait velocity (Figure 2E, right panel).
evidence: Multiple regression analysis showing interaction between age, frailty, and gait velocity.

claim: Age and energetic costs were the only explanatory variables for gait speed.
source: Of all the experimental variables analyzed, age and energetic costs were the only explanatory variables for gait speed (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Multiple regression analysis identifying significant predictors of gait speed.

claim: Mice from Group A (12–20 mo) were significantly heavier than group Y (7 mo) and group O (26–36 mo) animals as they entered the metabolic cages.
source: Mice from Group A (12–20 mo) were significantly heavier than group Y (7 mo) and group O (26–36 mo) animals as they entered the metabolic cages (Figure 2H).
evidence: Body weight measurements at the time of metabolic cage assessment.

claim: The higher ambulatory activity during the dark cycle was significantly lower in group O mice.
source: Lastly, the higher ambulatory activity during the dark cycle was significantly lower in group O mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—source data 2)
evidence: Metabolic cage measurements showing reduced activity in old mice.

claim: Depending upon the organ, a total of 133 to 177 metabolites was detected.
source: Depending upon the organ, a total of 133 to 177 metabolites was detected.
evidence: Metabolomics analysis results describing the number of detected metabolites.

claim: Combining univariate and multivariate statistics, 49 metabolites were identified that were significantly different in serum and across organs as a function of age, of which 46 were shared.
source: Combining univariate and multivariate statistics we identified 49 metabolites that were significantly different in serum and across organs as a function of age, of which 46 were shared.
evidence: Statistical analysis of metabolomics data identifying significantly changed metabolites.

claim: The liver was the organ exhibiting the highest abundance of metabolite intermediates from all major pathways involved in macronutrient metabolism and redox-related pathways.
source: The liver was the organ exhibiting the highest abundance of metabolite intermediates from all major pathways involved in macronutrient metabolism (glucose, lipids, amino acids) and redox-related pathways (nicotinamide, glutathione, pentose phosphate)
evidence: Metabolomics analysis showing relative metabolite abundances across organs.

claim: Several metabolites from redox-related pathways, such as pentose-phosphate, NAD+ salvage, methionine cycle, and transsulfuration, exhibited significant differences with age.
source: several metabolites from redox-related pathways, such as pentose-phosphate, NAD+ salvage, methionine cycle, and transsulfuration, exhibited significant differences with age
evidence: Metabolomics analysis identifying age-related changes in specific metabolic pathways.

claim: Brain and heart exhibited a net separation between the three groups of mice in partial least squares discriminant analysis.
source: As revealed by partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLSDA), a supervised clustering method, brain and heart exhibited a net separation between the three groups of mice.
evidence: Multivariate statistical analysis showing metabolic differences between age groups.

claim: In liver, skeletal muscle and serum, young and old animals were clearly separated while group A mice partially overlapped with both groups.
source: In contrast, in liver, skeletal muscle and serum, Y and O animals were clearly separated while group A mice partially overlapped with both groups (Figure 4B).
evidence: PLSDA analysis showing patterns of metabolic separation between age groups.

claim: G6P, ribulose 5P, ribose 5P and glutathione were elevated with age in liver and/or heart.
source: Specifically, G6P, ribulose 5P, ribose 5P and glutathione were elevated with age in liver and/or heart (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Metabolomics data showing age-related increases in specific metabolites.

claim: Serum metabolite profiles from old mice showed accumulation of intermediates from urea cycle function and significant accumulation of the branched-chain amino acids valine, isoleucine and leucine.
source: Serum metabolite profiles from old mice showed accumulation of intermediates from urea cycle function (urea, glutamine, ornithine), a pattern consistent with predominant amino acid degradation in the liver, and significant accumulation of the branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) valine, isoleucine and leucine (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Metabolomics analysis of serum showing age-related metabolic changes.

claim: The three top-ranked metabolites, glucose, 3-hydroxybutyrate, and glycerol appear to be lower in the serum of old mice.
source: Remarkably, the three top-ranked metabolites, glucose, 3-hydroxybutyrate (3-HB, a ketone body), and glycerol appear to be lower in the serum of old mice, suggesting a reduced supply of these fuel substrates from liver and adipose tissue to heart, brain, and skeletal muscle (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Metabolomics data showing reduced levels of key metabolites in old mice.

claim: In liver, depletion of glucose, pyruvate, sorbitol, fructose 1P, xylitol, maltose, and maltotriose with age suggests active glycolysis and glycogen breakdown.
source: In liver, depletion of glucose, pyruvate, sorbitol, fructose 1P (F1P), xylitol, maltose, and maltotriose with age suggests active glycolysis and glycogen breakdown, less utilization of the polyol pathway, and hepatic release to the circulation (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Metabolomics data with interpretation of metabolic pathway activity.

claim: The heart shows a remarkable accrual of BCAAs with age.
source: The heart shows a remarkable accrual of BCAAs with age.
evidence: Metabolomics analysis showing age-related accumulation of branched-chain amino acids in heart.

claim: Higher levels of the tricarboxylic acid intermediates fumarate, malate, and succinate suggest active mitochondrial function in the heart.
source: Higher levels of the tricarboxylic acid intermediates fumarate, malate, and succinate suggest active mitochondrial function.
evidence: Metabolomics data with inference about mitochondrial activity based on TCA cycle intermediates.

claim: In the brain, the accumulation of the top-ranked fatty acid ω6 linoleic acid together with stearic and palmitoleic acids is notably associated with the increased abundance of 3-HB.
source: In the brain, the accumulation of the top-ranked fatty acid ω6 linoleic acid together with stearic and palmitoleic acids is notably associated with the increased abundance of 3-HB, a preferred substrate of this organ (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Metabolomics data showing coordinated changes in fatty acids and ketone bodies in brain.

claim: The skeletal muscle from old mice exhibits high glucose catabolism as suggested by the accumulation of maltose, lactate and maltotriose.
source: Expectedly, the skeletal muscle from old mice exhibits high glucose catabolism as suggested by the accumulation of maltose, lactate and maltotriose.
evidence: Metabolomics data with inference about glucose metabolism in skeletal muscle.

claim: As mice age, organs such as liver and heart remodel their metabolism toward higher expression/activity of redox-related metabolic pathways.
source: Together, these data suggest that as mice age, organs such as liver and heart, which are exposed to higher oxidative stress as a result of their function (detoxification in the liver and energy generation in the heart), remodel their metabolism toward higher expression/activity of redox-related metabolic pathways, for example, pentose phosphate, NAD+ salvage and transsulfuration.
evidence: Interpretation of metabolomics data showing organ-specific metabolic remodeling with age.

claim: Skeletal muscle and brain do not appear to be able to remodel redox-related pathways thus becoming more vulnerable to increased oxidative stress with aging.
source: Oppositely, skeletal muscle and brain do not appear to be able to remodel those pathways thus becoming more vulnerable to increased oxidative stress with aging.
evidence: Interpretation of metabolomics data suggesting differential capacity for metabolic adaptation.

claim: Gait speed decline is a major functional biomarker of aging in mice.
source: This analysis demonstrated that (i) gait speed decline, which appears to be fully explained by age and frailty, is a major functional biomarker of aging in mice
evidence: Summary statement based on multiple analyses showing strong relationship between gait speed and aging.

claim: The deterioration of locomotor activity is associated with a dramatic increase in the energetic cost of physical activity from age approximately 19 months.
source: the deterioration of locomotor activity is associated with a dramatic increase in the energetic cost of physical activity from age ~19 months, and was paralleled by a sustained decrease of working capacity
evidence: Summary of metabolic treadmill data showing age-related changes in energy expenditure.

claim: Depletion of glucose, 3-HB, and glycerol in serum from old mice is consistent with reduced supply of these fuel substrates from liver and adipose tissue to other organs.
source: depletion of glucose, 3-HB, and glycerol in serum from old mice is consistent with reduced supply of these fuel substrates from liver and adipose tissue to other organs
evidence: Interpretation of metabolomics data suggesting impaired substrate supply with aging.

claim: Aging in mice favors up-modulation of glucose metabolism in cardiac and skeletal muscle as well as in liver.
source: aging in mice favors up-modulation of glucose metabolism in cardiac and skeletal muscle as well as in liver, where gluconeogenesis and urea cycle are also enhanced, as well as similar but less pronounced pattern in brain.
evidence: Summary of metabolomics findings showing tissue-specific metabolic changes with age.

claim: Physical performance metrics have provided important information about individualized estimates of survival as evidenced by the association of age-related decline in gait speed with reduced overall survival in humans.
source: For instance, physical performance metrics have provided important information about individualized estimates of survival as evidenced by the association of age-related decline in gait speed with reduced overall survival in humans (Studenski et al., 2011; White et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to human studies.

claim: Mice develop many of the histopathological characteristics of human aging during their lifespan, such as lymphocyte infiltration, tissue inflammation and necrosis, cancer, and amyloidosis.
source: Mice develop many of the histopathological characteristics of human aging during their lifespan, such as lymphocyte infiltration, tissue inflammation and necrosis, cancer, and amyloidosis (Mitchell et al., 2016; Mitchell et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about mouse aging characteristics supported by citations.

claim: The frailty index is a compilation of 31 clinical parameters, with 0 being not frail and one being frail.
source: The frailty index (FI) is a compilation of 31 clinical parameters, with 0 being not frail and one being frail (Whitehead et al., 2014).
evidence: Definition of the frailty index measurement with citation.

claim: The values obtained from FI assessment increased progressively among different groups of mice, passing from 0.13 ± 0.01 in group Y to 0.24 ± 0.01 in group A, and 0.31 ± 0.02 in group O.
source: The values obtained from FI assessment increased progressively among different groups of mice, passing from 0.13 ± 0.01 in group Y to 0.24 ± 0.01 in group A, and 0.31 ± 0.02 in group O (Figure 1B)
evidence: Quantitative frailty index measurements across age groups.

claim: Age accounted for 52.5% and 46.5% of the mean and maximal tail height variation, respectively.
source: Age accounted for 52.5% and 46.5% of the mean (p=2.61e-13) and maximal (p=1.87e-11) tail height variation, respectively (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing the proportion of variance explained by age.

claim: The effects of frailty on muscle strength were maintained after correction for age.
source: The effects of frailty on muscle strength were maintained after correction for age, indicating the presence of independent risk factors beyond chronological age that could reduce physical performance in the oldest mice.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing independent effect of frailty on muscle strength.

claim: Only a weak association existed between fasting blood glucose and the FI score.
source: In contrast to physical performance measurements, only a weak association existed between fasting blood glucose and the FI score (Figure 1M).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing weak correlation between glucose and frailty.

claim: A weak positive association was observed between fasting glucose levels and percent body fat.
source: whereas a weak positive association was observed between fasting glucose levels and percent body fat (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Correlation analysis between glucose and body composition.

claim: The whole-body lean tissue percentage was largely preserved during aging.
source: The whole-body lean tissue percentage was largely preserved during aging (p=2.15e-05, r2 = 0.250) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Body composition analysis showing minimal change in lean mass with age.

claim: There was a lower percentage of fat around the tibia per unit of body mass in animals of increased age.
source: Remarkably, there was a lower percentage of fat around the tibia per unit of body mass in animals of increased age, with the oldest group of mice being the most affected (p=0.002, r2 = 0.248)
evidence: Micro-CT analysis showing age-related changes in regional fat distribution.

claim: The percentage of lean tissue surrounding the tibia trended higher in group O compared to group A.
source: whereas the percentage of lean tissue surrounding the tibia trended higher in group O compared to group A (Figure 2C).
evidence: Micro-CT analysis showing age-related changes in regional lean tissue.

claim: The running VO2 values did not differ over the entire activity episode across age, thus ruling out a role for fatigue in the higher energetic cost in the oldest mice.
source: The running VO2 values did not differ over the entire activity episode (800 s.) across age, thus ruling out a role for fatigue in the higher energetic cost in the oldest mice (data not shown).
evidence: Analysis of oxygen consumption during exercise ruling out fatigue as a factor.

claim: RER varies between approximately 0.7 (predominant use of fats as fuel source) and 1.0 (exclusive carbohydrate utilization).
source: Respiratory exchange ratio (RER, defined as VCO2/VO2) varies between ~0.7 (i.e. predominant use of fats as fuel source) and 1.0 (i.e. exclusive carbohydrate utilization), with intermediate RER values implying mixed substrate use.
evidence: Definition of RER and its interpretation based on established physiological knowledge.

claim: The differences in work economy and heat production between the three age groups were maintained after adjusting for lean mass.
source: The differences in work economy and heat production between the three age groups were maintained after adjusting for lean mass (data not shown).
evidence: Statistical analysis controlling for body composition.

claim: At higher energetic costs there was a stronger decreasing relationship between gait velocity and age.
source: Moreover, at higher energetic costs there was a stronger decreasing relationship between gait velocity and age (Figure 2G, left panel).
evidence: Multiple regression analysis showing interaction between energetic cost, gait velocity, and age.

claim: There was a marked positive association between gait velocity and energetic costs in groups Y and A, whereas no significant relationship was observed in group O.
source: There was a marked positive association between gait velocity and energetic costs in groups Y and A, whereas no significant relationship was observed in group O (Figure 2G, right panel).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing age-dependent changes in the relationship between gait velocity and energetic costs.

claim: Distinctive diurnal patterns of O2 consumption and CO2 production were observed in the three groups of mice.
source: Distinctive diurnal patterns of O2 consumption and CO2 production were observed in the three groups of mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Metabolic cage measurements showing circadian patterns in respiratory parameters.

claim: EE was greater in group A compared with the other two groups consistent with their higher O2 consumption.
source: Moreover, EE was greater in group A compared with the other two groups consistent with their higher O2 consumption (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Metabolic cage data showing age-related differences in energy expenditure.

claim: The diurnal changes in RER in the three age groups showed statistically significant differences in the dark cycle between group Y vs. group O and group A vs. group O.
source: The diurnal changes in RER in the three age groups showed statistically significant differences in the dark cycle (D) between group Y vs. group O and group A vs. group O (Figure 2J)
evidence: Statistical comparison of RER values between age groups during dark phase.

claim: No difference in RER could be observed in the light phase between the different groups of mice.
source: No difference in RER could be observed in the light phase between the different groups of mice.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no significant differences in RER during light phase.

claim: There were no differences between groups Y and O mice in any of the measures except for the ambulatory activity.
source: In contrast, there were no differences between groups Y and O mice in any of the measures except for the ambulatory activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Statistical comparisons showing selective differences between young and old mice.

claim: Body weight was positively correlated with EE, oxygen consumption, and CO2 production.
source: As expected, body weight was positively correlated with EE, oxygen consumption, and CO2 production (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Correlation analysis between body weight and metabolic parameters.

claim: ANCOVA analysis demonstrated statistically significant differences in the relationship between body weight and respiratory parameters when comparing group Y vs. A mice and group Y vs. O mice.
source: This analysis demonstrated statistically significant differences in the relationship between body weight and respiratory parameters when comparing group Y vs. A mice and group Y vs. O mice.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing age-dependent changes in the relationship between body weight and metabolism.

claim: Visceral fat accumulation is associated with insulin resistance.
source: Visceral fat accumulation is associated with insulin resistance (Girard and Lafontan, 2008; Hardy et al., 2012)
evidence: Statement about the relationship between visceral fat and insulin resistance supported by citations.

claim: Subcutaneous fat plays a role in reducing insulin levels and improving insulin sensitivity.
source: while subcutaneous fat plays a role in reducing insulin levels and improving insulin sensitivity (Tran et al., 2008; Shuster et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about the metabolic effects of subcutaneous fat supported by citations.

claim: The increase in body fat percentage from young to adult mice was coincident with a greater subcutaneous/visceral fat ratio.
source: Here, the increase in body fat percentage from young to adult mice was coincident with a greater subcutaneous/visceral fat ratio, which, in turn, was associated with a significant drop in circulating insulin levels and HOMA-IR.
evidence: Analysis showing coordinated changes in body composition and metabolic parameters.

claim: The oldest mice had the highest ratio of subcutaneous-to-visceral fat and a likelihood of being insulin sensitive.
source: Noteworthily, the oldest mice had the highest ratio of subcutaneous-to-visceral fat and a likelihood of being insulin sensitive (lowest HOMA-IR).
evidence: Body composition and metabolic measurements in old mice.

claim: The rising energetic cost of walking is associated with steeper decline in gait speed in the elderly.
source: The rising energetic cost of walking is associated with steeper decline in gait speed in the elderly (Schrack et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about human aging supported by citation.

claim: The cost of running depends upon the animal's size rather than the speed at which an animal runs.
source: Specifically, the VO2 / gait speed ratio (in mL O2/Kg/m) is energetically and physiologically consistent with the energetic cost of, for example, walking or running (Figure 2D), to the extent that the cost of running depends upon the animal's size rather than the speed at which an animal runs (Taylor et al., 1970; reviewed in Schmidt‐Nielsen, 1984).
evidence: Statement about exercise physiology supported by citations.

claim: All hallmarks of aging exhibit prominent anabolic and catabolic effects.
source: All hallmarks of aging exhibit prominent anabolic and catabolic effects (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about aging hallmarks supported by citation.

claim: This was a cross-sectional study in male C57Bl/6N mice rather than a longitudinal study.
source: This was a cross-sectional study in male C57Bl/6N mice rather than a longitudinal study of male and female mice of different genetic background which would have accounted for genetic variability and sex.
evidence: Description of study design and its limitations.

claim: Animal rooms were maintained at 22.2 ± 1°C and 30–70% humidity.
source: Animal rooms were maintained at 22.2 ± 1°C and 30–70% humidity.
evidence: Description of animal husbandry conditions.

claim: The lights were turned off at 6:00 PM and back on at 6:00 AM each day.
source: The lights were turned off at 6:00 PM and back on at 6:00 AM each day.
evidence: Description of light cycle used in the study.

claim: Mice were group-housed up to four per cage with ad libitum access to food and drinking water.
source: Mice were group-housed up to four per cage with ad libitum access to food (Teklad Global 18% Protein Extruded Rodent Diet, #2018S, Envigo, Frederick, MD) and drinking water.
evidence: Description of housing and feeding conditions.

claim: There were three age groups of mice, in months: Young, 3–8 (n = 23); Adult, 13–23 (n = 27); and Old, 27–36 (n = 23).
source: There were three age groups of mice, in months: Young, 3–8 (n = 23); Adult, 13–23 (n = 27); and Old, 27–36 (n = 23).
evidence: Description of experimental groups and sample sizes.

claim: Two mice, one adult (A) and one old (O), died during experimentation, bringing the final number of groups A and O mice to 26 and 22, respectively.
source: Two mice, one adult (A) and one old (O), died during experimentation, bringing the final number of groups A and O mice to 26 and 22, respectively.
evidence: Description of attrition during the study.

claim: Metabolomic analysis was performed by the West Coast Metabolomics Center at UC Davis in brain, heart, liver, skeletal muscle, and serum from nonfasted animals.
source: Metabolomic analysis was performed by the West Coast Metabolomics Center at UC Davis (Davis, CA) in brain, heart, liver, skeletal muscle, and serum from nonfasted animals as previously described (Mitchell et al., 2018; Mitchell et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of metabolomics methodology with citations.

claim: HOMA-IR was calculated to assess group differences in insulin resistance using the HOMA2 Calculator software.
source: Homeostasis model assessment-insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) was calculated to assess group differences in insulin resistance using the HOMA2 Calculator software available from the Oxford Centre for Diabetes, Endocrinology and Metabolism Diabetes Trials Unit website (http://www.dtu.ox.ac.uk/homacalculator/index.php).
evidence: Description of method for calculating insulin resistance.

claim: No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size.
source: No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size.
evidence: Statement about study design regarding sample size determination.

claim: p Value ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
source: p Value ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
evidence: Statement of statistical significance threshold used in the study.
